plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 3: Polynomial and Rational Functions
plan.contextChunk: This figure graphs a rational function on a coordinate plane and marks the two distinct ways its graph breaks. The horizontal axis is labeled x and ticked at odd values from -3 through 9; the vertical axis is ticked at even values from -6 to 6 over a dotted gray grid. The teal curve comes in two branches. The left branch enters from the far left almost flat and just above the x-axis, carries a small hollow open circle at x equal to -1 marking a point removed from the graph, then descends through the x-axis at x equal to 1 and drops steeply, running off the bottom of the frame as it approaches x equal to 3. The right branch begins high just to the right of x equal to 3, falls quickly, then levels off toward the right edge near y equal to 1. A red dashed vertical line stands at x equal to 3, labeled below the axis in red as Vertical asymptote at x = 3. A blue annotation at the upper left reads Removable discontinuity at x = -1, with a thin arrow to the open circle. Setting the hollow dot against the dashed line is the contrast being drawn: one break is a single missing point, the other sends the curve toward infinity on both sides.

interactionPlan.concept: A rational function can break in two fundamentally different ways: a removable discontinuity (a single missing point where a factor cancels) and a vertical asymptote (where the function grows without bound because a denominator factor does not cancel).
elements: x-axis labeled 'x', ticked at odd values -3, -1, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
y-axis labeled 'y', ticked at even values -6 through 6
dotted gray grid across the plotting region

teal left branch of the rational function: nearly flat just above the x-axis from the far left, crossing the x-axis at x = 1, then dropping steeply toward negative infinity as x approaches 3 from the left
teal right branch: starting high just right of x = 3, falling quickly, leveling off toward y ≈ 1 at the right edge
hollow open circle on the left branch at (-1, ~0.5) marking the removed point
blue annotation 'Removable discontinuity at x = -1' with a thin arrow to the open circle
red dashed vertical line at x = 3
red label 'Vertical asymptote at x = 3' below the axis
trace point marker on the curve with live (x, y) readout (slider-driven)
cancelled-factor annotation showing (x + 1)/(x + 1) in the factored form near the hole

interactions.label: Highlight break
interactions.teaches: The two breaks are categorically different: one is a single missing point on an otherwise continuous branch, the other is a line the curve can never touch as it shoots off to infinity

interactions.label: x approaches 3
interactions.teaches: As x approaches 3 from either side, |y| grows without bound — the function has no finite value to 'fill in', which is exactly why a vertical asymptote cannot be repaired like a hole

interactions.label: Show cancelled factor
interactions.teaches: The factor (x + 1) appears in both numerator and denominator and cancels, leaving the branch continuous everywhere except the single point x = -1 — the hole is one missing function value, not a break in the curve's shape

demo_steps.title: Spot the hole
demo_steps.narration: The left branch looks like one smooth curve, but the open circle at x = -1 marks a single point where the function simply has no value. Every other point on the branch is intact.

demo_steps.title: Why the hole is removable
demo_steps.narration: Reveal the factored form: the factor (x + 1) cancels from numerator and denominator, so the curve is continuous — only the lone function value at x = -1 is missing.

demo_steps.title: Approach the asymptote
demo_steps.narration: Highlight the dashed line at x = 3 and drag the trace point toward it from the right: y climbs higher and higher. From the left, y plunges downward. No finite value could ever fill this break.

demo_steps.title: Contrast the two breaks
demo_steps.narration: Set the trace point exactly at the hole's neighborhood and compare: at x = -1 the y-values settle to a finite limit (one point fixable), while at x = 3 the values explode (no fix possible).

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A cancelled factor removes exactly one point (a hole, fixable by redefining a single value); an uncancelled denominator factor creates a vertical asymptote where the function grows without bound and no value can be assigned.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Coordinate plane with x from about -4 to 10 and y from -7 to 7, dotted light-gray grid, axes labeled x and y in italics. The teal curve models f(x) = (x - 1)/((x - 3)) with a hole at x = -1 (i.e., numerator and denominator share an (x+1) factor): left branch asymptotic to y ≈ 1 on the far left, open circle at (-1, 0.5), crossing the x-axis at x = 1, then diving to -∞ as x → 3⁻; right branch descending from +∞ just right of x = 3 and leveling toward y = 1. Red dashed vertical line at x = 3 with the red label beneath the x-axis at the right; blue 'Removable discontinuity at x = -1' annotation upper-left with a thin arrow to the open circle. When a break is highlighted, the open circle or the dashed line brightens/enlarges while the other dims. The slider drives a glowing trace point clamped to the curve (side chosen automatically by x < 3 or x > 3) with a small live readout of (x, f(x)); as |x - 3| shrinks the readout should visibly blow up. The factor-view toggle overlays the factored expression showing (x + 1) struck through in both numerator and denominator, positioned near the hole with a connecting arrow.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between removable discontinuity and vertical asymptote; the learner switches the highlighted break, the open circle or dashed vertical line brightens, and the contrast between a missing point and unbounded behavior becomes clear.
- Slider for x approaching 3; the learner moves a trace point toward the vertical asymptote from either side, the y-value shoots downward or upward, and it becomes clear why x = 3 is not a removable hole.
- Toggle factor-cancelled view: the learner reveals the cancelled factor that fixes the removable discontinuity at x = -1, keeping the hole in place while showing that only one function value is missing from an otherwise continuous branch.

authoredContext:
Notice that x+1 is a common factor to the numerator and the denominator. The zero of this factor, x=−1, is the location of the removable discontinuity. Notice also that x–3 is not a factor in both the numerator and denominator. The zero of this factor, x=3, is the vertical asymptote. See the figure.

Graph of f(x)=(x^2-1)/(x^2-2x-3) with its vertical asymptote at x=3 and a removable discontinuity at x=-1.
